headline: Jersey Protects Over a Fifth of Its Seas From Destructive Fishing
meta_description: The Isle of Jersey expanded marine protections to 21.7% of territorial waters, shielding vulnerable habitats while working with its fishing industry.
summary_short: Jersey doubled down on ocean conservation, protecting 21.7% of its seas from trawling while partnering with fishers on sustainable alternatives.
body:
The Isle of Jersey has expanded protections across its territorial waters in a move that demonstrates how conservation and fishing can coexist. Starting September 1st, 21.7% of Jersey's seas became off-limits to trawling and other damaging fishing practices—a 15% increase from previous protections. The self-governing bailiwick, which administers its own environmental laws while coordinating with French and British authorities, is targeting some of the English Channel's most structurally complex and vulnerable habitats. These zones serve as critical feeding grounds and nurseries for fish stocks and other marine biodiversity that the island depends upon.

Jersey's leadership frames this not as a sacrifice for the fishing industry, but as an investment in its future. The government is actively working with fishers to develop alternative fishing areas that are less ecologically sensitive, recognizing the economic pressures commercial operators face. Francis Binney, Jersey's head of marine resources, emphasized that "protecting important habitats today helps ensure Jersey's waters remain productive and biologically rich in the future." This balance reflects a broader scientific consensus: marine protected areas around the world consistently demonstrate that preserving the richest marine environments actually increases fish stocks in surrounding exploitable waters—ultimately making them more valuable to the fishing industry than unrestricted commercial access would be.

Managed through Jersey's Marine Spatial Plan and developed in consultation with French authorities, the expanded protections represent pragmatic stewardship. As Jersey's Minister for the Environment Mary Le Hegerat noted, the island's seas are "one of the island's greatest natural assets." The real story here isn't a win for conservation at fishing's expense—it's evidence that healthy oceans and thriving fisheries aren't competing goals, but interdependent ones.
quick_facts: Jersey expands marine protections from 6.7% to 21.7% of territorial waters
New protections ban trawling and damaging fishing practices starting September 1st
The bailiwick coordinates environmental policy with French and British authorities
Protected zones serve as nurseries and feeding grounds for fish stocks
